# **Deep Temporal Generalization: Architecture, In-Context Learning Mechanics, and the Evaluation of Time Series Foundation Models**

The forecasting paradigm has undergone a profound structural shift, transitioning from localized, task-specific deep networks to large-scale, zero-shot Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs).1 Historically, classical supervised architectures like PatchTST, DLinear, or Autoformer required training a bespoke model from scratch for every unique target dataset, incurring prohibitive computational overhead and restricting horizontal scalability across diverse industrial domains.1 By pretraining on massive multi-domain corpora spanning hundreds of billions to trillions of time points, modern TSFMs attempt to capture the underlying "grammar" of temporal dynamics.2 This allows these models to execute direct zero-shot transfer to unseen physical distributions without any downstream parameter updates.1  
However, translating the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) to the temporal domain is complicated by distinct physical and statistical constraints.3 Unlike natural language, which features structured vocabularies and discrete tokens, time series data is characterized by varying sampling frequencies, extreme non-stationarity, high-dimensional cross-variate dependencies, and strict causality requirements.3 To address these challenges, two prominent architectural pathways have emerged: attention-based, patch-tokenized Transformers designed for parallel long-horizon forecasting, and recurrent state-tracking models built on extended Long Short-Term Memory (xLSTM) backbones optimized for low-latency, constant-memory streaming inference on the edge.6

## **Comparative Taxonomy and Architectural Mechanics of Modern TSFMs**

The structural design of a TSFM reflects a balance between parameter scale, computational complexity, and target domain conditions.6 While general-purpose models seek broad cross-domain generalization, specialized observability models prioritize high-dimensional, sparse telemetry, and recurrent architectures focus on streaming efficiency.3  
To illustrate these trade-offs, the specifications of prominent model families are detailed below.

| Model Variant | Core Neural Backbone | Parameters (Active / Total) | Context Window Limit | Primary Mixing Mechanism | Probabilistic Interface | Pretraining Corpus Volume |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **TimesFM 1.0 / 2.0** 6 | Decoder-only Transformer | 500M | 2,048 | Patch-based self-attention | Parametric / Quantile | 100 Billion points (Google Trends, Wikipedia, Synthetic) 6 |
| **TimesFM 2.5** 6 | Decoder-only Transformer | 200M | 16,384 | Patch-based self-attention with residual MLP tokens | Optional 30M quantile head (up to 1k horizon) | Expanded multi-domain search & web telemetry 6 |
| **Toto 1.0** 3 | Decoder-only Transformer | 151M | 512 | Proportional factorized space-time attention (11:1 ratio) 14 | Student-T Mixture Model (SMM) 14 | 2.36 Trillion points (43% Datadog telemetry, public, synthetic) 14 |
| **Toto 2.0 (Frontier)** 10 | Decoder-only Transformer | 2.5B (Scaling family: 4M to 2.5B) | 4,096 | Alternating time/variate attention 10 | 9-level direct quantile head (![][image1] to ![][image2]) 10 | 1.0 Trillion points (75% real-world telemetry, synthetic) 5 |
| **TiRex 1.0 / 1.1** 8 | Stacked xLSTM (sLSTM Blocks) | 35M | 2,048 | Recurrent state tracking with Contiguous Patch Masking 8 | Direct multi-quantile probabilistic grid 18 | High-diversity univariate and synthetic corpora 18 |
| **TiRex-2** 9 | Stacked xLSTM (sLSTM & mLSTM) | 38.4M (Univariate) / \+44.1M (Multivariate) | 8,192 | Bidirectional time mixer & asymmetric grouped variate mixer 9 | Direct multi-quantile probabilistic grid 18 | Synthetic multivariate coupling & LOTSA data 12 |

### **Tokenization and Step-Reduction Mechanics in TimesFM**

Google’s TimesFM utilizes a decoder-only Transformer backbone that maps continuous temporal sequences into discrete token representations using patch-based tokenization.6 To map raw observations to high-dimensional transformer embeddings, TimesFM processes the input series through a multilayer perceptron (MLP) block with residual connections, concatenating the resulting tokens with positional encodings.6 The model’s main objective is next-patch prediction: given an input patch of time-points, the stacked self-attention layers learn to forecast the subsequent contiguous block.6  
A key technical characteristic of TimesFM is its support for asymmetric input and output patch lengths.6 In typical autoregressive text models, token generation proceeds step-by-step.10 In temporal forecasting, however, generating long horizons point-by-point can lead to severe error accumulation and high computational latency.6 TimesFM mitigates this by pretraining with an output patch length that is larger than the input patch length.6  
For example, a model trained with an input patch length of 32 and an output patch length of 128 can resolve a 256-step future horizon in just two forward passes.6 In the first step, the model uses the historical context to forecast points 257 to 384\.6 In the second step, the newly predicted output is concatenated with the historical input to forecast points 385 to 512\.6 This step-reduction strategy limits autoregressive drift, resulting in structurally coherent long-horizon forecasts.6  
The TimesFM architecture has evolved from its legacy 500M parameter configurations (versions 1.0 and 2.0) to the optimized 200M parameter TimesFM 2.5.6 This latest iteration extends the context window capacity to 16k tokens and introduces continuous quantile forecasting up to a 1k horizon via an optional 30M parameter quantile head, eliminating the need for explicit frequency indicators.6

### **Space-Time Attention and Parameter Scaling in the Toto Family**

Datadog's Toto family is optimized for multivariate cloud infrastructure telemetry.3 Machine telemetry—comprising metrics like CPU saturation, database query rates, memory consumption, and API latency—is characterized by high cardinality, extreme sparsity, and complex cross-metric correlations.3 A standard multivariate Transformer that flattens all metrics and timestamps into a single attention map incurs a quadratic computational cost of ![][image3], where ![][image4] is the number of variables and ![][image5] is the context length.9  
To address this complexity, Toto 1.0 introduced proportional factorized space-time attention.14 The model architecture routes data through alternating self-attention blocks, using an 11:1 ratio of time-wise attention blocks to variate-wise attention blocks.14 This design prioritizes temporal processing within individual metrics while periodically allowing cross-variate updates to capture system-wide correlations.14  
Toto 2.0 optimizes this by utilizing alternating time/variate attention layers.10 This mechanism dynamically routes cross-variate dependencies without flattening the entire multivariate grid, making it well-suited for high-dimensional observability workloads.10  
Furthermore, Toto 2.0 is trained using Maximal Update Parametrization (![][image6]\-![][image7]), establishing a scaling family that spans from 4M to 2.5B parameters.5 The use of ![][image6]\-![][image7] ensures that optimal hyperparameters—such as learning rates, weight decay, and attention scaling—remain stable across different model widths.10 This mathematical framework allows developers to perform hyperparameter optimization on small, computationally inexpensive proxy models and transfer the resulting configurations directly to the 2.5B parameter frontier checkpoint, ensuring stable scaling behavior.10

### **Recurrent State Tracking in the TiRex Family**

NX-AI's TiRex models present a non-Transformer alternative for zero-shot forecasting, built on extended Long Short-Term Memory (xLSTM) backbones.8 While Transformers can capture long-range global context, they do not maintain a compressed recurrent state, requiring full-history recomputation as new observations arrive.9 TiRex leverages the state-tracking capabilities of sLSTM and mLSTM modules to compress past temporal histories into a fixed-size memory state.8 This recurrent design allows the model to process streaming sequential data with constant update costs.9  
The first-generation TiRex utilizes sLSTM blocks combined with Contiguous Patch Masking (CPM) to deliver zero-shot predictions with a compact 35M parameter footprint.7 TiRex-2 scales this approach to multivariate streaming scenarios.9 It activates a 38.4M parameter path for univariate inputs and engages an additional 44.1M parameter path for multivariate forecasting, supporting joint dependencies and covariate conditioning.9  
The temporal dynamics are managed by a bidirectional xLSTM time mixer, while cross-variate correlations are processed by an asymmetric grouped-attention variate mixer.9 This decoupled architecture enables TiRex-2 to capture cross-channel interactions and condition on future-known covariates (such as holiday calendars or scheduled maintenance) while preserving strict target-causality and maintaining constant-memory streaming performance.9

## **The In-Context Learning and Training-Time Masking Paradigms**

The concept of In-Context Learning (ICL) has been central to the design of general-purpose time series models, though its implementation and limitations differ significantly from those in natural language processing.21

### **The Theoretical Mechanics of Time Series In-Context Learning**

In natural language processing, ICL is an emergent property of scale, where models learn to perform novel tasks from context prompts without parameter updates.21 This capability is widely theorized to function as an implicit meta-optimization process where the forward pass of self-attention layers acts as an implicit gradient descent algorithm.21  
However, applying this framework to TSFMs reveals key conceptual differences.21

| Dimension | Natural Language Processing (NLP) | Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Emergence vs. Engineering** | Emergent property of scale; spontaneously develops in large decoder architectures.21 | Explicitly engineered; relies on inductive biases and structured pretraining tasks.21 |
| **Mechanistic Process** | Simulates a meta-dataset-specific optimizer executing gradient descent in the forward pass.21 | Explicit structural routing (e.g., Chronos-2's group attention, TiRex-2's asymmetric mixers).11 |
| **Input Vocabulary Constraints** | Unbounded semantic vocabularies mapped to high-dimensional discrete token spaces.21 | Bounded continuous values; restricted by physical scale shifts and non-stationarity.3 |
| **Pretraining Alignment** | Unsupervised next-token prediction over raw web corpora.21 | Explicitly structured multi-task contexts (e.g., TimesFM’s ICTP, TiRex-2's synthetic coupling).6 |
| **Theoretical Limits** | Bounded by sequence length constraints and attention span limits. | Bounded by the information compression limit of a single univariate sequence.21 |

Rather than relying entirely on emergent scale-driven properties, modern TSFMs often use engineered structural biases to capture contextual dependencies.21 For example, Chronos-2 implements "group attention," which explicitly shares representation states across related series within context groups during pretraining.2 This engineered routing helps the model learn cross-series dynamics on the fly, bypassing the information compression limits of single-series univariate forecasting.21

### **Synthetic Data and Pretraining Design**

To teach foundation models the "grammar" of time series, developers frequently combine real-world data with synthetic time series generated via statistical models or physical simulations.2 For instance, TimesFM is trained on a mixture of synthetic patterns and real-world datasets like Google Trends and Wikipedia pageviews.6 This synthetic pretraining helps the model learn fundamental properties like seasonality, trend decomposition, and noise handling.6  
However, over-reliance on synthetic data carries risks.21 While mathematically defined synthetic series provide clean gradient signals during training, they often lack the complex non-stationarity, sudden structural breaks, and heavy-tailed noise of real-world environments.3 If a pretraining corpus is dominated by overly simplistic synthetic curves, the model may struggle when deployed on noisy real-world distributions, such as low-voltage energy grids or distributed server networks.1

### **The Convergence on Contiguous Patch Masking**

A key development in reducing error propagation in zero-shot models is the transition from step-by-step autoregressive decoding to Contiguous Patch Masking (CPM).8 In traditional autoregressive forecasting, a model predicts a single future step, appends this prediction to its input context, and repeats the process.10 This step-by-step approach is prone to compounding errors, where a small prediction error at step ![][image8] propagates and distorts the trajectory of subsequent steps.6  
To address this, both TiRex and Toto 2.0 utilize CPM during pretraining.8 The training mechanics of CPM proceed as follows:

1. The input time series is segmented into a sequence of non-overlapping patches.8  
2. During training, continuous, multi-patch spans of the sequence are randomly masked.8  
3. The core model backbone is trained to reconstruct the entire masked, contiguous span of future patches in parallel.8  
4. During inference, the target forecasting horizon is treated as a set of mask tokens, allowing the model to decode the entire future sequence in a single forward pass.10

This parallel reconstruction strategy avoids step-by-step autoregressive re-computation, resulting in lower inference latency and structurally coherent long-horizon trajectory predictions.8

## **Handling Non-Stationarity, Scale Shifts, and Sparsity in Telemetry Data**

Cloud observability metrics represent a challenging domain for time series forecasting.3 Telemetry streams are rarely stationary and are frequently dominated by high-sparsity regimes, extreme heavy-tailed spikes, and sudden structural shifts driven by system deployments, autoscaling events, or hardware incidents.3 Furthermore, the physical variables span vast differences in scale, where a request rate may jump from dozens to millions per second while a parallel error rate remains near zero.5  
To establish stable zero-shot forecasting across these varied operational regimes, Toto incorporates several specialized data-processing and architectural components.3

### **Causal Patch Normalization**

In general-purpose time series models, instance normalization is commonly used across the entire context window to stabilize training.14 However, normalizing an entire input sequence during autoregressive forecasting can introduce future data leakage, where statistics from the end of the context window influence the normalization of earlier steps.14  
To prevent this leakage, Toto implements causal patch normalization.14 The running mean and standard deviation are calculated causally, restricted to the history up to the final timestep of each individual patch.14 Let the input multivariate series be represented as ![][image9], where ![][image10] is the number of channels/variates and ![][image5] is the context length. The sequence is divided into non-overlapping patches of size ![][image11]. For patch ![][image12] and channel ![][image13], the causal mean ![][image14] and standard deviation ![][image15] are calculated strictly using historical observations up to the final timestep of that patch 14:

This causal formulation prevents future leakage while stabilizing the patch representations fed to the transformer.14

### **Robust Causal Scaling via the Arcsinh Transformation**

To process metrics spanning several orders of magnitude without losing the signal of near-zero variations, Toto 2.0 replaces standard linear scaling with an inverse hyperbolic sine (![][image19]) transformation 10:  
![][image20]  
This mathematical function exhibits linear behavior near zero, which preserves the subtle fluctuations of low-valued metrics, but transitions to logarithmic scaling for larger values, compressing extreme spikes.10 This helps prevent dominant numerical outliers from destabilizing the gradient flow during pretraining.10

### **Quantile Output Heads for Operational Alerting**

While Toto 1.0 utilized a parametric Student-T Mixture Model (SMM) output head to model heavy-tailed distributions, Toto 2.0 implements a direct, non-parametric quantile output head.10 SMMs can suffer from numerical instability when exposed to highly irregular, sparse telemetry streams.14  
The quantile head in Toto 2.0 directly outputs nine distinct quantile levels from ![][image1] to ![][image2].10 This non-parametric approach accommodates skewed and multi-modal distributions without requiring the estimation of continuous distribution parameters.10 For operations teams, these quantiles map directly to service-level objectives (SLOs), capacity planning, and dynamic anomaly thresholds (such as identifying when a resource metric exceeds its predicted ![][image2] boundary).5

## **Computational Efficiency, Streaming, and Edge-Capabilities**

The deployment of TSFMs in real-world industrial settings, such as manufacturing lines, power grids, and edge devices, highlights a key limitation of Transformer backbones: the computational footprint of self-attention.9

### **The Computational Overhead of Self-Attention**

Because self-attention requires calculating pairwise dependencies across all historical steps, its computational complexity scales quadratically as ![][image21], where ![][image5] is the context length.9 In continuous streaming environments where new telemetry or sensor observations arrive sequentially, a Transformer must concatenate the new step, discard the oldest step, and re-compute the entire attention matrix of the context window.9 This full-history recomputation leads to high latency and energy consumption, which can limit its suitability for edge hardware such as Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs).9

### **Recurrent State Tracking via xLSTM**

To address these streaming constraints, the TiRex family utilizes a recurrent backbone built on extended Long Short-Term Memory (xLSTM) networks, incorporating both scalar sLSTM and matrix mLSTM modules.8 This recurrent state-tracking design acts as a lossy, constant-memory compression of historical context.9  
When a new observation patch arrives in a streaming setup, the internal hidden state is updated incrementally with constant ![][image22] computational complexity per patch, bypassing the full-history recomputation required by Transformer backbones.9  
To enable multivariate forecasting and accommodate covariates without compromising streaming efficiency, TiRex-2 implements a factorized design 9:

* **Bidirectional Time Mixer:** Processes individual sequences using parallel, bidirectional xLSTM modules to capture past temporal trends.9  
* **Asymmetric Grouped-Attention Variate Mixer:** Integrates future-known covariates (such as promotions, calendar markers, or scheduled maintenance) alongside past target histories.9 This asymmetric grouping mechanism allows targets to attend to covariates while preventing future target values from leaking backward in time, preserving causal relationships.9

### **Scalable Multivariate Pretraining via Synthetic Coupling**

Pretraining high-capacity multivariate models typically requires vast amounts of joint multi-channel data, which are often less abundant than univariate datasets.9 To overcome this data limitation, TiRex-2 introduces a synthetic coupling pipeline.9 During pretraining, the pipeline constructs diverse multivariate training samples on the fly from large univariate corpora.9  
It does this by dynamically grouping unrelated univariate series and injecting explicit cross-variate dependency structures, such as direct linear mixtures, lagged causal relationships, and indirect joint drivers.2 This synthetic augmentation exposes the model to a wide variety of cross-variate patterns, enhancing its zero-shot generalization to real-world multivariate datasets.9

### **Edge Hardware Benchmarks**

The physical efficiency of the recurrent xLSTM design has been validated on industrial edge hardware.13 In hardware tests conducted on industrial PC units (such as those from KEBA) with limited RAM (ranging from 2 GB to 16 GB), TiRex (35M parameters) was evaluated against Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, and PatchTST-FM.13

* **Latency and Throughput:** TiRex achieved faster inference times than Chronos-2, supported by its recurrent hidden-state updates that avoid quadratic attention map scaling.23  
* **Energy Consumption:** Because it avoids full-history attention recomputation, TiRex required less energy per forecast step than its Transformer-based counterparts.23  
* **Accuracy-to-Footprint Ratio:** In evaluations using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) on the GIFT-Eval benchmark, TiRex matched the accuracy of larger models while maintaining a smaller parameter footprint, making it highly competitive for on-device industrial edge deployment.7

## **Downstream Application, Evaluation Challenges, and the Evaluation Crisis**

The evaluation of TSFMs often reveals a performance gap between standardized benchmarks and messy, real-world deployments.4 This discrepancy has led to closer scrutiny of benchmark validity and downstream evaluation methods.1

### **The Evaluation Crisis and Benchmark Integrity**

A recurring challenge in time series literature is the "evaluation crisis," where highly parameterized foundation models occasionally fail to outperform simple, non-trainable statistical baselines (such as naive seasonal models or ETS) or basic linear models (like DLinear) on standard academic benchmarks.4 This issue is often exacerbated by data contamination, where evaluation datasets are inadvertently included in the pretraining corpora of massive models, artificially inflating their zero-shot performance scores.1  
To address this challenge and ensure fair evaluation, contemporary research emphasizes strict data decontamination protocols.19 For example, the TiRex-2 release includes specific decontaminated checkpoints 19:

* **TiRex-2-g:** Excludes all datasets from the GIFT-Eval benchmark from its pretraining corpus to ensure clean zero-shot testing.19  
* **TiRex-2-f:** Excludes all evaluation datasets from the fev-bench suite, allowing for unbiased zero-shot evaluation on multivariate tasks.19

These decontaminated variants provide a more accurate assessment of a model's true generalization capabilities on genuinely unseen downstream distributions.19

### **Downstream Case Study: Low-Voltage Load Forecasting**

A practical validation of zero-shot TSFM capabilities is presented in a downstream study on short-term net load forecasting across 200 real-world low-voltage (LV) electrical feeders.1 This domain is highly complex due to the decentralized integration of renewable generation and electric vehicle charging, which introduces high volatility and non-stationarity at the feeder level.1  
The study compared Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and TabPFN-TS against six fully trained baseline models using the FeederBW dataset, which was published after the training cutoff of the evaluated TSFMs.1

* **Zero-Shot Generalization:** Chronos-2 demonstrated superior performance in generating probabilistic quantile forecasts, effectively generalizing to the unseen physical feeder behaviors without site-specific fine-tuning.1  
* **Robustness to Covariate Omission:** In ablation studies where local weather covariates were omitted, Chronos-2 adapted by expanding its predictive uncertainty bands.1 It successfully leveraged the historical load context to infer proxy weather-driven seasonal patterns, demonstrating robust zero-shot adaptation.1  
* **Application-Oriented Metrics:** To align model evaluation with the operational priorities of distribution system operators (DSOs), the study introduced a peak-focused KPI based on the physical characteristic curve of a grid fuse.1 In low-voltage grid management, planning is dictated by peak loads to prevent fuse failure and asset damage.1

Rather than relying solely on abstract statistical metrics like Mean Absolute Error (MAE), this application-oriented metric links peak forecast errors directly to a trade-off model:  
![][image23]  
This formulation allows utility boards to directly translate zero-shot probabilistic forecasts into operational risk and financial planning metrics.1

## **Strategic Synthesis and Future Deployment Pathways**

The structural differences between current time series foundation models provide a framework for matching model architectures to specific operational environments and computational constraints.6  
To assist in architectural selection, the table below maps operational constraints and domain characteristics to the most suitable model families.

| Primary Operational Constraint | Domain Characteristics | Recommended Model Class | Specific Checkpoint / Family |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Strict Resource & Memory Limits** (e.g., PLCs, Edge PCs, on-device IoT) 13 | Streaming univariate or multivariate sensor data with known future schedules 9 | Recurrent xLSTM-based architectures 8 | **TiRex-2** (38.4M \- 82.5M params) 9 |
| **High-Scale, Distributed Infrastructure** (e.g., Cloud Platforms, Kubernetes Networks) 5 | High-cardinality, sparse, and noisy multi-metric telemetry 3 | Decoder-only space-time Transformers 10 | **Toto 2.0** (313M \- 2.5B scaling family) 10 |
| **Centralized Business & Operations Planning** (e.g., Demand Forecasting, Retail Planning) 6 | Low-to-medium cardinality series with long historical context 6 | Patch-tokenized general-purpose Transformers 6 | **TimesFM 2.5** (200M params with 16k context) 6 |

Additionally, emerging research suggests moving toward unified latent prototype spaces rather than modeling raw physical variables directly.2 Advanced models like Falcon-X decouple heterogeneous physical quantities and map them to a dimension-agnostic coordinate system using Differential Prototype Attention.2 This latent-space approach helps align physical properties across different datasets, improving zero-shot knowledge transfer.2  
For organizations managing diverse operations, a model-routing layer can optimize deployment.16 Under this strategy, general business series are routed to patch-based models like TimesFM 2.5, machine telemetry is processed by Toto 2.0, and high-frequency edge streaming is handled by recurrent backbones like TiRex-2.6 This routing approach balances model capacity and computational efficiency across the enterprise.16
